summary: Registers the Enumservice voice, with the subtype tel, following the IANA process from RFC 3761. It indicates that the URI produced can be used to start an interactive voice call. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM links phone numbers to internet contacts. This adds a label meaning that this contact can be called with voice.

questions: what is the enum voice enumservice
what is a tel uri in enum
how does enum find a phone number contact
subtitle: A label in ENUM that says a phone number can be dialed for a live, two-way voice call.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps telephone numbers to contact URIs in DNS, but a record needs a standard label saying what kind of communication the URI supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the Enumservice "voice" with the subtype "tel" under the IANA process from RFC 3761, so a NAPTR record can say its tel: URI starts an interactive voice call.
tldr.outcome: A client can treat a NAPTR with this Enumservice as the owner's statement that they can take a voice call at that number, placed through the PSTN or PLMN. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 4415 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Enumservices and the Voice Registration
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping, RFC 3761) turns an E.164 telephone number into a domain name. It then uses DNS features, such as NS delegation and NAPTR records, to look up the communication services available for that name.

An Enumservice is a label placed in the services field of a NAPTR record. It has a type and an optional subtype. The type says what kind of communication session can be started with the URI in the record. The subtype names the subsystem used to start it and is usually tied to the URI scheme. Both type and subtype, where present, must be supported for a correspondent to use the NAPTR.

An Enumservice only has meaning inside the "E2U" DDDS application that ENUM defines. This RFC registers the Enumservice "voice" with the subtype "tel".
sections.plainLanguage: A label on a phone book entry says what you can do with it. The label has a big kind, like voice, and a small kind that says how to reach it, like tel.

sections.title: What the Voice Enumservice Means
sections.content:
The registration sets the name, type and subtype all to the values "voice", "voice" and "tel", with the URI scheme tel:. The functional specification calls the communication "Interactive Voice". It is expected to involve bidirectional media streams carrying audio data.

A client may infer that the person who controls the NAPTR is saying they can take an interactive voice session when contacted through the generated URI. The intended usage is COMMON.
sections.plainLanguage: If you see this label, you can guess the person is happy to talk on the phone at that number.

sections.title: How a Client Places the Call
sections.content:
The registration says the owner of the NAPTR is reachable through the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) or a Public Land Mobile Network (PLMN) at the number in the URI. The subsystem needed is a "Dialer". A Dialer either connects locally to the PSTN or PLMN or reaches them indirectly, and it uses the number in the URI to place a voice call to a network that routes by E.164 numbers.

The connection may be indirect. The user may have a provider that accepts call requests over an IP-based protocol such as SIP or H.323 and places the call to the PSTN through a remote gateway. That provider either accepts tel: URIs or has a way to convert them to a protocol-native form.

The tel: value SHOULD be fully qualified, using the global phone number form of RFC 3966. A local phone number SHOULD NOT be used unless the zone controller is sure that every client able to read the record can resolve it unambiguously and route a call to it from their network access points.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone app reads the number and dials it. The call may go through a helper company that connects it to the regular phone network. Always write the full number, with the country code, so nobody dials the wrong place.

sections.title: Example NAPTR Record
sections.content: The RFC gives one example record. Under the origin 0.6.9.2.3.6.1.4.4.e164.arpa., the entry 3.8.0 holds a NAPTR with order 10 and preference 100, the flag u, and the service E2U+voice:tel. Its regular expression replaces any input with tel:+441414960000.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is one phone book line. It says: for this number, the service is voice, and the thing to dial is the full phone number.

sections.title: Privacy and Cost Risks
sections.content:
DNS is a global, distributed database, so anything stored in it is visible to anyone anonymously. The RFC notes this is not qualitatively different from a telephone directory, but people can have their data collected automatically without knowing it. Harvested numbers can be used to send "junk faxes" or "junk SMS". Unlike an email address, a phone number cannot easily be made "sacrificial", because a single E.164 number or fixed range is usually tied to each PSTN access.

People whose data is published MUST give explicit informed consent. They should also know that removing data does not remove copies taken by harvesters, so any publication may be permanent. Regulations in many regions will require that they can request removal at any time and that their consent is confirmed at regular intervals.

Calling over the PSTN or a PLMN may cost the caller money, and premium rate numbers can cost far more than a normal call. The originating user SHOULD be shown the destination number so they can decide whether to place the call.

The security considerations of RFC 3761 and the DNS threats in RFC 3833 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting your number in a public list means anyone can copy it, even people who send junk. Also, calling some numbers costs a lot, so the app should show you the number first.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has registered the Enumservice "voice" with a single subtype "tel", following the framework in RFC 3761. The RFC defines this Enumservice and the behavior expected of clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The keeper of internet name lists wrote the new label into the official list.
